, geminin küçük bir yatma sonrasında yat: is the situation where the ship's angle of heel continues to increase after a small heel. Such a state of balance is extremely dangerous in practice and can lead to the ship capsizing.

When these conditions are met, the rule gives a reasonable approximation; However, in many ports these conditions are not met.
12’ler kuralı, altı saatlik standart gel: The rule of 12s approximates the rate at which water height changes over the standard six-hour tidal cycle. The tide changes 1/12 of the Range in the first hour; 2/12 in the second hour; 3/12 in the third hour; 3/12 in the fourth hour; 2/12 in the fifth hour; 1/12 in the sixth hour. Total 12/12 = full range, that is, the transition from HW to LW or LW to HW is completed.
12’ler kuralı, LW’den HW’ye veya HW’den:
The rule of 12s is a practical mnemonic rule that gives an approximation of the ratio of the water height change to the total range occurring each hour in a standard six-hour tidal cycle from LW to HW or HW to LW. The basic premise of the rule is that the tidal curve is close to sinusoidal and therefore changes fastest at mid-tide and slowest at the ends (around HW and LW).

Rule: the total range (HW − LW) is divided into 12 equal parts. The change occurring every hour is at the rates of 1/12, 2/12, 3/12, 3/12, 2/12, 1/12, respectively. The sum of these ratios is 12/12 = 1 (full range). The method is extremely practical, especially for fast and visual calculations; It is possible to draw in a notebook or do mental calculations.

The signal includes the ship's identity (MMSI or registration number), GPS position (if equipped with a GPS module) and distress status. COSPAS-SARSAT satellites receive this signal and transmit it to LUT (Local User Terminal) stations, which transmit it to the relevant MRCC (Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre). With GPS-integrated EPIRB, position accuracy drops to approximately 100 m; In models without GPS, location is determined by the Doppler effect, which is slower and less accurate (2–5 km). EPIRB additionally emits a 121.5 MHz homing signal, allowing aircraft and helicopters to be guided at close range.

Heavy weather navigation is a special navigation regime in which certain speed, route and operation decisions are made in order to protect the structural integrity, stability and crew safety of the ship in strong wind and wave conditions. The fundamental principle of this regime is that ship safety is always the first priority, despite ETA or commercial calendar pressure.

Heavy weather navigation is not a purely reactive approach; It is an ambitious foresight and decision process. Before entering a heavy weather zone, a good navigator interprets meteorological data, evaluates route alternatives, and determines the speed-route combination that will manage heavy weather with the least risk.

This document limits possible liabilities to the crew and provides critical evidence for insurance processes. Protest preparation, incident diary (log records), witness statements and timely notary application are made with the coordination of the captain. Informing the P&I Club (protection and indemnity insurance) as soon as possible is also part of this process.

Ağırlık merkezi, gemiyi oluşturan tüm ağ: The center of gravity is the point where all the weights that make up the ship are considered to be collected at a single point and the direction of action of the weight force passes. This point is one of the most critical elements that determine the stability character of the ship, and every loading, unloading, ballasting or ballasting process performed on the ship changes the location of the center of gravity. The center of gravity is not a fixed geometric point; It is displaced in vertical, longitudinal and transverse directions depending on the current loading status of the ship.

On the other hand, lowering the center of gravity makes the righting arms larger and makes the ship behave more stable. For this reason, it is vital for stability that ballast tanks are located at lower levels, heavy loads are stacked as low as possible and the free surface effect is kept under control. The concept of center of gravity forms the basis of all stability analyses, from metacentric relations to righting moment calculations, and is treated as the first parameter taken into account in every calculation.

Vertical position is expressed as the distance measured from the spine upwards and is usually denoted KG. Longitudinal position is usually evaluated as the distance to the bow or stern, with reference to the midsection. Transverse position refers to the distance in the port or starboard direction relative to the center line of the ship. Appraisal is the first and fundamental stage of the passage planning process within the framework of IMO A.893(21). At this stage, all information specific to the cruise is systematically collected, its updates are checked and it forms the basis for the planning phase. A passage plan prepared without appraisal means that it is built with incomplete or incorrect assumptions and jeopardizes safety.

Bridge Resource Management (BRM), köprüü: Bridge Resource Management (BRM) is a management system that ensures coordinated and effective work of the bridge team.

Bridge Resource Management (BRM) is the discipline of ensuring ship safety by using all the resources of the bridge team — people, technology, information and procedures — in the most effective way. Derived from the Crew Resource Management (CRM) concept developed in aviation in the 1970s, BRM aims to reduce the role of human error in more than 80% of maritime accidents. With IMO's STCW Manila Amendments (2010), BRM training has been made mandatory at all maritime qualification levels. BRM; It is a holistic approach that includes not only technical skills but also leadership, situational awareness, communication quality and decision-making processes. Understanding BRM is critical for maritime faculty students to contribute to bridge safety both during the exam process and from the first days of their careers.

Especially in maneuver decisions, the FORDEC model (Facts, Options, Risks/benefits, Decision, Execution, Check) or similar structured frameworks are used. The culture of team members 'not being afraid to ask questions' ensures that errors are caught early. COLREG (Collision Regulations), denizde: COLREG (Collision Regulations) is a set of international rules that all ships must comply with in order to prevent collisions at sea.
COLREG (Convention on the International: COLREG (Convention on the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972) is an international convention prepared within IMO and entered into force in 1977 to prevent collisions, which are the most destructive type of maritime accidents. COLREG, consisting of 38 rules and annexes, is valid in all waters, including offshore and harbor entrance channels; Without prejudice to the jurisdiction of countries that have rules specific to inland water only. The rules are built on three pillars: constant and effective lookout (Rule 5), safe speed determined by the conditions (Rule 6) and the risk of conflict identified and managed at an early stage (Rules 7–8). All these technical rules are complemented by the 'good maritime practice' general provision of Rule 2: if strict adherence to the rules in unusual circumstances creates danger, the captain may take the initiative. For maritime students, COLREG is the basic legal framework that governs daily situations in both examination and real sea life.

The ship, which is stationary but whose machinery is running, emits two long blasts in succession. Sailing and fishing vessels that do not steer, have limited maneuverability, and have limited draft due to their draft, give one long and two short blasts. The towed ship (if present) gives one long and three short blasts immediately after the towing ship. A rapid bell rings at the bow of the ship at anchor (5 seconds, once a minute); On ships longer than 100 m, a gong is additionally sounded at the stern. Giving these signs correctly and on time is mandatory for both safety and legal liability.

Crossing (kesişme) durumu, COLREG'in en: The crossing situation is one of the most frequently encountered and also one of the most misinterpreted scenarios of COLREG. If two motor ships are cutting each other's route at the same time in a way that creates a risk of collision and this situation does not fall within the scope of head-on or overtaking, Rule 15 comes into play. Crossing figures prominently in maritime accident statistics worldwide: incorrect ship assignment (which is the 'give-way'), late or inadequate maneuvering and miscommunication over VHF are major sources of error. For maritime faculty students, understanding the crossing scenario with its geometric, legal and operational dimensions is one of the most critical competencies in STCW exams and real sea life.

The combination of fixed bearing + decreasing range indicates the risk of conflict. Calculating the close passage point (CPA) and TCPA of the other ship with the relative vector on the ARPA is the most accurate way to determine the time required for the give-way maneuver. In practice, it is standard to take action when TCPA > 15 minutes; Leaving it later may force the stand-on ship to perform a Rule 17(b) manoeuvre. It is sometimes difficult to determine which ship is 'starboard' in the rule: if two ships are on almost the same course and intersect at a small angle difference, the head-on–crossing distinction can create a gray zone.

The righting arm forms the geometric basis of the righting moment and directly reflects the angular change of the stability behavior of the ship.

DOP (Dilution of Precision Coefficient) is the numerical indicator of the effect of satellite geometry on position accuracy in GNSS systems. DOP does not directly affect measurement accuracy; It shows how measurement errors become position errors due to geometry. A low DOP value means that the satellites are geometrically well positioned and a small measurement error will lead to a small position error.

HDOP (Horizontal DOP) shows the sensitivity dilution in the horizontal position (latitude and longitude). In maritime navigation, HDOP is the most critical type of DOP because the ships' primary concern is horizontal position; Altitude information is usually of secondary importance. durumu, aynı kargo miktarını taşıyan gem: This represents the scenario where the ship carrying the same amount of cargo reaches the destination port after consuming fuel, fresh water and consumables throughout the cruise. In this case, fuel tanks are generally reduced to 10% reserve level. Fuel consumption can significantly change the position of the ship's center of gravity; KG may increase or decrease, especially depending on the location of the fuel tanks. For this reason, the arrival state must also meet the stability criteria independently.
durumu, geminin kargo olmaksızın yalnızc: This is the scenario where the ship sails with only ballast water and no cargo. Having full ballast tanks ensures adequate propeller sinking and bow draft remains at acceptable levels. In the case of ballast, the displacement is low and the wind surface area of ​​the ship is large; Therefore, the wind heeling moment becomes more critical. Since the KM value differs at low displacements, separate stability evaluation is mandatory for ballast cases.
durumu, geminin maksimum kargo kapasites: This is the scenario where the ship leaves the port at maximum cargo capacity, with 100% fuel and fresh water and all consumables fully loaded. This generally corresponds to the highest displacement and creates a critical scenario for stability as the VCG (vertical center of gravity) potential is highest. In case of full load departure, draft and trim values ​​must not exceed the loadline limits and all IMO stability criteria must be met.
durumu, uzun bir balast seyiri sonrasınd: This is the scenario in which the destination port is reached with minimum fuel after a long ballast cruise. This usually corresponds to the lowest displacement value and can be the weakest point in terms of stability. In the case of minimum fuel, the position of the center of gravity changes and the GM value may approach critical levels.

Plane navigation is an approach in which the spherical shape of the Earth is considered negligible at short distances and navigation calculations are made with plane geometry. ECDIS (Electronic Chart Display and Information System) is an advanced bridge navigation system that integrates electronic navigational charts (ENC - Electronic Navigational Chart) with ship sensor data, which can officially replace the paper chart, provided that it meets IMO standards. It became mandatory gradually between 2012 and 2018 with the SOLAS Part V regulation; Passenger ships of 10,000 GT and above and commercial ships of 3000 GT and above must carry ECDIS.

The main value of ECDIS lies in its continuous and automatic comparison between geographical location (GPS/GNSS) and map hazards. The system generates an alarm when the ship approaches a dangerous area. However, this power also leads to a dangerous trap called 'automation reliance': the navigator's over-reliance on ECDIS and the relegation of manual verification and independent thought. Many maritime accidents in recent years have been caused by procedural errors in the use of ECDIS.

ECDIS (Electronic Chart Display and Information System) is an electronic navigation system that is considered the legal equivalent of a paper map. It must comply with IMO MSC.232(82) performance standards.

The proliferation of electronic navigation systems has required the bridge to manage multiple digital information streams. Cross-checking is based on the principle of verifying each source by comparing location and environmental information obtained from different and independent sources. This principle directly addresses the danger of blind reliance on a single sensor and is essential to meet COLREG's obligation of proper watchdog.

Cross-checking is not just a 'good practice'; It is a procedure clearly prescribed in the IMO and STCW guidelines on electronic navigation. SOLAS Chapter V Regulation 19 requires the use of suitable means of navigation and verification of their reliability. The discipline of cross-checking allows the navigator to recognize system errors and GPS/ECDIS anomalies before they become real dangers.

Gelgit (tide), Ay ve Güneş’in yerçekimse:
Tide is the periodic rise and fall of the water level in the oceans and seas due to the gravitational influence of the Moon and the Sun. This effect is astronomically predictable, so tide tables can be calculated long periods in advance. The tide shows different characters around the world: in some ports it rises and falls twice a day (semidiurnal), in others it rises and falls twice a day (diurnal), and in others a mixed cycle is observed.

The importance of tide in terms of maritime is multifaceted: tide information plays a critical role in areas such as port entry-exit timing, UKC (Under Keel Clearance) calculation, under-bridge passage height, coastal passage safety and water surface estimation in rescue operations. It is mandatory for maritime faculty students to know both the physical basis of the tide and the calculation methods from the tables.
Gelgit bilgisi UKC, tidal window ve köpr: Tide information is used directly in UKC, tidal window and bridge crossing calculations.
Gelgit hesabında doğrudan uygulama: Bir: Direct application in tide calculation: If the time corrections for spring and neap of a secondary port are given in different tables (for example +20 min for spring, +35 min for neap) and there is a period between spring and neap on that day, the HW height of the day is proportionally interpolated to a correction value.

Gelgit tabloları (tidal tables), belirli:
Tidal tables give each day's High Water (HW) and Low Water (LW) times and heights for a particular reference port (standard port), usually in UT (UTC) and in meters relative to the chart datum. Admiralty Tide Tables (ATT), publications of the Department of Navigation, Hydrography and Oceanography for Türkiye, and tables of local administrations are among the main sources.

Tide tables are organized in two basic structures: (1) Standard ports: Full annual HW/LW time and heights are given in tabular form. (2) Secondary/subordinate ports: Time and altitude correction factors are given relative to a standard reference port; These factors are applied to the tables of the standard port and the calculation is made for the secondary port.
Gelgit tabloları standart limanlar için: Tide tables give HW/LW times and heights in UT for standard ports.
Gelgit tablolarında spring ve neap arası: In tide tables, the transition between spring and neap can be traced from the systematic increase or decrease in each day's HW/LW height values. In almanacs or annual tables, the correlation between moon phases and tidal amplitude is clearly visible.

If the LAT datum is used, the tide height is always positive or zero (because LAT is the lowest level). If the actual water level had fallen below the LAT, the tide height would have been negative; This is an unusual situation.

Gelgitin ana kaynağı, Ay’ın Dünya üzerin: The main source of tides is the differential gravitational force of the Moon on the Earth. The Moon pulls more strongly on the water mass on the side closer to the Earth; The water swells on this side. On the other hand, a bulge forms on the opposite side of the Earth due to the centrifugal effect (the force resulting from the rotation around the center of gravity of the Earth-Moon system). This is why there are two opposing tidal swells on Earth at the same time.

In real sea cruising, a ship's SOG (Speed ​​Over Ground) and COG (Course Over Ground) values ​​do not depend only on engine power and rudder angle; Current (set and drift) and wind shear (leeway) also enter the equation. The vectorial combination of these three components creates the actual ground motion of the ship.

This combined effect makes the audience wonder 'should I be thinking about where I am?' It requires navigation by knowing 'where I'm going' instead. GPS COG and SOG directly measure this actual movement; However, when GPS is not available or GPS reliability is questioned, calculating these three components vectorially is the only option.

GMDSS dört deniz alanı tanımlar ve her a: GMDSS defines four sea areas, and each area is determined by the infrastructure technology that provides coverage. Area A1 is the area under DSC (Digital Selective Calling) coverage of at least one VHF shore station; its typical range is 20–30 nautical miles. Area A2 is the area outside A1 but under DSC coverage of an MF (Medium Frequency) coast station; its range typically extends to around 100–150 nautical miles. Area A3 is the area outside A1 and A2 but under Inmarsat satellite coverage; This coverage includes approximately 70°N – 70°S latitudes. Area A4 covers areas other than A1, A2 and A3; mainly in the polar regions, where HF (High Frequency) radio communication is the main means of communication.

GPS (Global Positioning System), Amerika:
GPS (Global Positioning System) is a space-based satellite navigation system developed by the American Department of Defense and opened to full capacity for civilian use since 1995. The system consists of at least 24 active satellites positioned in various orbits around the Earth, and these satellites constantly emit strong time signals. A receiver on Earth calculates its own position by receiving these signals.

The revolutionary importance of GPS in terms of maritime is that it offers continuous, automatic and high-accuracy position determination. GPS works day and night, in all weather conditions, in every ocean; The sextant has become a complement to radar and visual positioning and has become the primary data source of modern ECDIS systems.

However, GPS also carries the danger of blind trust. Interrupting, jamming or spoofing the signal coming from satellites can disable GNSS systems or cause incorrect location indication. Therefore, STCW and IMO define GPS as a supporting tool; navigators must maintain radar, astronomy and conventional positioning proficiency.

GPS alıcıları farklı DOP türlerini rapor: GPS receivers report different types of DOP. HDOP: horizontal position (latitude, longitude) – most important in sea navigation. VDOP: vertical position (altitude) – critical in aviation. PDOP (Position DOP): 3D position, √(HDOP²+VDOP²). TDOP: time accuracy. GDOP: Geometry DOP covers all components.
GPS alıcısı, her uydunun göndermekte old: The GPS receiver measures the time difference between the signal sent by each satellite and the copy signal produced by the receiver itself. This time difference is multiplied by the speed of light to calculate the distance to the satellite (pseudo-range). The term 'pseudo' indicates that the error in the receiver clock adds error to the distance.
GPS alıcısında oluşan toplam konum hatas: The total position error occurring at the GPS receiver is a combination of different error components. Satellite clock and orbit errors, atmospheric delays (ionosphere/troposphere), receiver clock error, multipath reflection and receiver noise magnify the total error. At moments when the satellite geometry is weak (high DOP), the same error size produces larger deviations in position.

Truth; It is the cumulative effect of multiple factors such as satellite clock errors, receiver clock error, ionosphere and troposphere delays, multipath signal propagation, and satellite geometry. GPS doğruluğunu etkileyen başlıca hata k: The main sources of error affecting GPS accuracy are: (1) Ionospheric delay: the ionosphere slows down the signal; dual frequency receivers can fix this. (2) Tropospheric delay: humidity and pressure in the lower atmosphere affect the signal. (3) Multipath: If the signal hits buildings or other structures and reaches the receiver through different paths, an error occurs; It becomes evident at port entrances and near cities. (4) Satellite geometry (DOP): if satellites are not well distributed in the sky, calculation accuracy decreases. (5) Ephemeris errors: small errors in the orbital parameters broadcast by satellites.

GPS’te trilaterasyon uygulaması şöyle iş: Trilateration in GPS works like this: each satellite broadcasts a message containing its position and signal sending time. When the receiver receives this signal, it calculates the pseudo-range to the satellite by multiplying the signal delay (Δt) by the speed of light (c). This so-called distance defines the sphere surface and indicates that the receiver is located somewhere on this sphere. The intersection of 3 spheres obtained with 3 satellites theoretically gives two points; The point outside the earth is automatically eliminated and the 3D position is obtained.

Height of Tide refers to how many meters above the chart datum the water level is at a certain time and port. Only HW and LW times and heights can be read directly from the tide table; The water height must be calculated for every moment in between.

This calculation can be done by three basic methods: (1) Rule of Twelfths: simple and fast, but approximate; (2) Sine curve interpolation: a more accurate mathematical method; (3) Admiralty tide curve (tidal curve): the most accurate method, used especially in ports with complex or irregular tidal profiles. The rule of 12 and the tidal curve method are generally required in maritime exams.

IMO Resolution A.893(21) came into force in 1999 under the title 'Guidelines for Voyage Planning' and sets out the voyage planning standards that should be applied on all ships operating international voyages. The decision divides cruise planning into four mandatory phases: Appraisal, Planning, Execution and Monitoring. These four stages ensure that the ship operates within a structured safety framework at every step from departure to arrival.

IMO A.893(21) becomes a legal obligation when considered together with SOLAS Chapter V Rule 34. SOLAS V/34 requires appropriate cruise planning to 'plan the journey and expectations in advance'. The application of these two regulations together defines passage planning as both a technical and legal obligation.

COLREG Rule 19 comes into play when fog, heavy rainfall, snow, sandstorms or other similar conditions restrict visibility. The main difference of Rule 19 from all other rules is that it applies to ships approaching without visual contact and eliminates the give-way / stand-on distinction — each ship must maneuver without having a full view of the opposing ship's position and intentions. While this makes radar reading, ARPA analysis and audio signals critical, it also creates a navigational environment where misinterpretations develop more quickly. For maritime students, all the requirements of Rule 19 — speed, radar, sound signals and maneuvering restrictions — must be understood in their entirety.

Kıyı seyri (Coastal Navigation), geminin:
Coastal navigation is a form of navigation in which the ship navigates within visual distance of the shore or within the scope of radar, and continuous position confirmation can be made. Compared to open sea navigation, it offers more safe reference points and involves more traffic, fewer squares and more danger. This contradictory feature makes coastal navigation techniques both a rich and critical subject.

The essence of coastal navigation techniques lies in the principles of determining a reliable position and ensuring sustainable safety. Instead of adhering to a single method, using visual reference, bearing, transit line, clearing line and electronic systems together creates a reliability hierarchy. When there is an error in one method, the other one steps in and reveals the error; This cross-validation approach should be applied throughout the course.

ECDIS, on the other hand, superimposes the electronic map with the GPS location and provides alerting based on dangers.

The '5 Whys Technique' interrogates the cause of each error at up to five layers to get to the root cause. Example: Why did the conflict occur? → The ship did not change course. Köprüüstünde basınç merkezlerini takip e: The most basic tool for monitoring pressure centers on the bridge is the barometer. A single instantaneous value provides little information on its own; What's really valuable is the 3-hour trend curve. A decrease of 1 hPa per hour or more indicates an approaching strong low pressure system or front and requires immediate action. During shift handovers, the barometer trend must be conveyed verbally and in writing. The location, movement direction and speed of the pressure centers on the synoptic map are recorded in the route plan and the operation calendar is arranged accordingly. Köprüüstünde cephe geçişine hazırlık sis: Preparation for the front crossing on the bridge should be systematic. The estimated passage time of the front is recorded in the route plan; At least 2 hours before this time, deck security is increased and external operations are stopped or accelerated. The wind shift direction and size are evaluated in advance and a maneuver alternative is prepared. If low visibility is expected, COLREG limited visibility procedures are activated. The engine room is alerted to the need for low speed or full power. During frontal passage, the frequency of radar, AIS and visual surveillance is increased.

'Minimum safe shift personnel' regulated under STCW Rule VIII/2 and the bridge organization determined within the framework of the IMO MSC Circular constitute the legal basis for workload management. Procedurally, critical tasks are shared to avoid ‘single point failure’: the officer monitoring the navigation chart and the officer monitoring VHF traffic must be different people. If the person in the navigator role looks at many screens at the same time and undertakes more than one task, the risk of 'tunnel vision' (focusing on a single task) increases.

This article also envisages the profile of a captain who evaluates and judges the situation in its entirety rather than blindly following the rules. Although COLREG rules give clear instructions for certain situations (crossing, head-on, overtaking), it is not possible to foresee all scenarios in the open sea; Rule 2 closes this loophole. In practice, the concept of 'good maritime practice' is widely used in court decisions: what would a reasonable captain do in these circumstances? Internalizing this standard provides a much more permanent professional competence than memorizing the rules.

Risk is determined by the compass method (fixed compass direction) or CPA/TCPA values ​​calculated by ARPA. A ship whose compass does not change runs the risk of collision; If CPA is approaching zero and TCPA is decreasing, the risk is high. The key phrase of the rule is 'if there is doubt, there is risk' — this principle forces conservatism. Rule 8 prescribes three basic criteria for preventive manoeuvres: (1) the maneuver must be made early; (2) the maneuver must be executed with wide angle and clarity (small rudder changes mislead the opposing ship); (3) A new risk of conflict should not be created as a result of the maneuver. The principle of 'early and evident' is the indispensable concept of COLREG; It is essential to take action well before a last-minute Rule 17(b) maneuver is expected.

Leeway (wind drift) is the phenomenon in which the actual path (COG - Course Over Ground) followed by the ship, under the influence of wind force, deviates towards the leeward from the route indicated by the ship's heading. In other words: although the ship steers in a certain direction, the wind pushes it laterally and the actual track deviates from the intended course.

Leeway is expressed in degrees and is always in the leeward direction; That is, in a northerly wind (upwind = north, leeward = south) the ship slides south. The magnitude of the Leeway angle; It depends on wind strength, ship's freeboard height, speed and ship form.

Factors that reduce the leeway angle: full load condition, high speed, a narrow and deep ship hull.
Leeway açısının sayısal olarak belirlenm: Numerical determination of the leeway angle is necessary for route and heading calculation in cruise planning. Metasentrik nokta, geminin küçük yatma a: The metacentric point is one of the basic geometric reference points used to define the stability behavior of the ship under small heel angles. When the ship is upright, the direction of the buoyant force is represented by a vertical line passing through the center of buoyancy. When the ship tilts at a very small angle, the center of buoyancy shifts to a new position and the direction of buoyancy passing through this new point intersects with the initial direction at a point. This intersection point is called the metacentric point and is usually denoted by the letter M.
Metasentrik nokta, yalnızca küçük yatma: The metacentric point is a concept that is valid only for small angles of repose and is therefore used in “initial stability” or “small angles stability” analyses. As the angle of repose increases, the path followed by the center of lift ceases to be linear and the metacentric approach loses its validity. The metacentric point therefore defines the initial heeling behavior of the ship, not the large angles stability.
Metasentrik yüksekliğin büyüklüğü, gemin: The size of the metacentric height also determines the movement character of the ship. Ships with very large GM values ​​are called “hard” ships; These ships make fast and short-term rolling movements. This may increase structural loads and negatively affect personnel comfort. In contrast, ships with very small GM values ​​are defined as “soft” ships; Periods of roll are long and the ship exhibits slow, reluctant movements. Excessively small GM values ​​bring the risk of loss of stability.

Monitoring – Passage Planning Dördüncü A: Monitoring – Phase Four of Passage Planning
Monitoring (İzleme), passage planning sü:
Monitoring is the final phase of the passage planning process and continues throughout the journey. At this stage, the compliance of the navigation plan with the actual application conditions is regularly checked; When deviations are detected, the reasons are investigated and necessary corrective measures are taken. Monitoring is not a reactive alarm management; It is a proactive compliance monitoring process.

The effectiveness of monitoring is directly related to the situational awareness of the bridge team. The officer who notices the deviation must understand its cause (current, wind, loss of speed, aiming error?), assess its extent, and take appropriate corrective action in a timely manner.
Monitoring kapsamındaki temel parametrel: Basic parameters within the scope of monitoring: (1) Position: GPS COG and location; It is verified at regular intervals by radar fix or visual confirmation. Position updates are made hourly in the open sea and frequently on the shore. (2) XTE: Instantly monitored on ECDIS; intervention occurs when the alarm threshold is exceeded. (3) SOG and ETA: Compared with planned speed and arrival time; Significant deviations require updating. (4) Meteorology: Barometer trend, visual observations and NAVTEX/SafetyNET messages are compared to plan expectations.
Monitoring sırasında tespit edilen bir s: A deviation detected during monitoring is handled through a systematic process: (1) Detect the deviation and measure its size (XTE amount, ETA difference, speed difference). (2) Recognize the cause: is the discharge stronger than expected? Is the wind in an unplanned direction? Loss of speed due to machine problem? (3) Determine corrective action: heading correction, speed adjustment or plan revision. (4) Inform the captain if necessary. (5) Save to log.

Paralel indeks (Parallel Index), radar v:
Parallel Index is a navigation tracking technique that plots parallel to the planned course line on the radar or ECDIS and continuously shows the horizontal distance between the ship and a fixed reference point (usually a prominent shore point, cape, lighthouse or radar reflector). The technique is very simple in essence: the ship's distance to a certain point is kept under control at all times by drawing a line parallel to the course line according to the position of that point on the radar or ECDIS screen.

The parallel index is one of the most critical navigation tools of the bridge, especially in narrow straits, approach routes of ports, shallow waters and situations where visibility is limited. Thanks to this technique, the officer can instantly see how much he has deviated from the planned route; Small deviations can interfere before they become larger. The fact that it can be applied with radar, even without a visual cue or if the GPS is corrupted, increases the reliability of the technique.

Parallel index implementation is based on the principle that the only truly useful cruise control is instantaneous, continuous, and visual verification. Just knowing the ship's location is not enough; It is necessary to make sure that the ship is moving in the right direction and at the right distance. Therefore, IMO and STCW legislation define the parallel index technique as a mandatory component of bridge qualification programmes.
Paralel indeks uygulamasında şu adımlar: The following steps are followed in the parallel index application: (1) Before the journey, the most appropriate reference point for each critical section of the route is selected on the map and the planned distances are measured. (2) These distances are recorded in the PI table or plan note and transferred at shift handover. (3) During navigation, the reflection of the reference point is detected on the screen and the PI line is adjusted to show that reflection. (4) If the reference point lags behind the line, the ship is moving away from the planned route; If it's in front of you, it means it's getting closer.
Paralel indeks, rotaya paralel çizilen r: The parallel index instantly monitors the ship-to-shore distance with a reference line drawn parallel to the route.

Passage planning (rota / sefer planlama):
Passage planning (route / voyage planning) is the comprehensive preparation process carried out before the cruise to ensure that the ship reaches the destination from the departure point safely, efficiently and in accordance with the legislation. IMO Resolution A.893(21) divides this process into four mandatory stages: Appraisal, Planning, Execution and Monitoring. This framework is also supported by SOLAS Chapter V; It creates a legal liability on the captain and navigation officers of all ships operating internationally.

The importance of route planning stems from the fact that it enables the bridge to operate 'proactively' rather than 'reactively' by identifying hazards and constraints in advance. When navigating without a plan, dangers are noticed as they approach; In these moments, both time and space for movement are limited. If there is a plan, the dangers are known well in advance, alternative decisions are made in advance, and the bridge can act decisively in times of crisis.

PDOP (Position Dilution of Precision) refers to the total geometric precision dilution in both horizontal and vertical position components of the GNSS receiver. PDOP is equal to the square root of the sum of the squares of HDOP and VDOP:

PDOP = √(HDOP² + VDOP²)

This relationship clearly shows that PDOP is always greater than or equal to HDOP; because when vertical uncertainty is added, the total position uncertainty increases. In marine navigation, PDOP provides an overview of 3D position accuracy; however, HDOP is often the primary monitoring parameter.

PSC müfettişi, gemiye çıkışından itibare: The PSC inspector requests certificates, security documents and important records from the captain and senior officer upon boarding the ship. In accordance with Regulation 34 of SOLAS Chapter V, the navigation plan must be prepared for each voyage and be accessible on the bridge. The audit takes place in two stages: in the first stage, certificates and documents are checked (document audit); In the second stage, physical equipment, procedures and records are examined (detailed audit). According to the Paris MOU criteria, ships with a high risk profile — based on flag, classification history and number of previous detentions — are subject to more frequent and more comprehensive inspections. Deficiencies are recorded as 'deficiency'; Deficiencies that exceed certain thresholds or are critical for safety will result in detention.

If ECDIS is used, additional checks come into play: ECDIS software must be certified and up to date, ENCs must be under current license, alarm thresholds must be set to appropriate values, and GPS datum compatibility with the datum used in ECDIS must be documented. Radar (Radio Detection And Ranging), mik:
Radar (Radio Detection And Ranging) is an active detection system that emits electromagnetic energy pulses in the microwave band (typically 3 GHz / S-band or 9 GHz / X-band) in the direction of the target and extracts the distance, bearing and movement information of the target by analyzing the reflected signal. Marine radar operates regardless of visibility; It can detect targets even in fog, rain, darkness or heavy sea spray conditions.

Maritime radar is the most critical electronic tool of the bridge. Under COLREG Rules 5 and 7, the use of radar is required for proper lookout and conflict risk assessment. SOLAS Chapter V requires ships of 500 GT and above to have at least two independent radars. Modern ARPA (Automatic Radar Plotting Aid) systems automatically track targets, calculate CPA and TCPA and generate alarms on the risk of conflict.
Radar anteni kısa süreli güçlü elektroma: The radar antenna sends short-term strong electromagnetic pulses and then goes into reception mode for a short time. This send–listen cycle is repeated hundreds of times per second. The distance to the target is calculated by measuring the time it takes for the sent pulse to hit a target and return (two-way travel time, t).

Radar mevki tayini (Radar Fixing), kıyı:
Radar fixing is the process of determining the exact location of the ship on the map using radar distances and bearings taken from the coastline or significant objects. In situations where GPS access is not available or is questioned, radar fix provides an independent and reliable position source. Radar locator is also used to verify GPS location.

The main advantage of fixing with radar is that it is based on real-world reference: radar detects physical objects in real time and is not dependent on GPS or map databases. Therefore, electronic map errors or GPS distortions do not negatively affect the radar fix. However, radar measurements also have their own systematic and random errors; It is the navigator's responsibility to understand and minimize these errors.

Radar paralel indeksi, köprüüstü seyir t:
Radar parallel index is one of the most practical and important applications of bridge navigation techniques. The basic idea is simple: a line is drawn on the radar screen representing the horizontal distance of a fixed reference point to the ship, and the ship tracks its position relative to this line throughout its course. As long as the reflection of the reference point on the radar screen remains above this line, the ship is on the correct course at the correct distance; Any deviation is immediately noticed visually.

Radar PI is the routine navigational monitoring tool of the bridge during coastal navigation, narrow strait crossings, port approaches and in limited visibility conditions. STCW qualification standards expect officers to have the ability to establish and interpret radar PI; MCA and IMO guidelines define this technique as an integral part of passage plan preparation.

Rhumb line veya loxodrom, tüm meridyenle:
Rhumb line or loxodrome is the surface curve that intersects all meridians at a constant angle. In other words, if the ship always sails at the same angle (true course) to the north-south meridians, the line it follows is loxodrome. The practical consequence of this technical definition is extremely powerful: there is no need to change the route throughout the journey; The rudder is held steady.

In the Mercator projection, a loxodrome appears as a straight line connecting the start and end point. This feature is one of the main reasons that makes the Mercator chart the standard for sea navigation: it is possible to draw and read the route directly on the chart using a ruler and protractor. This practicality makes the loxodrome the preferred line format for short and medium distance cruising.

However, due to spherical geometry, loxodrome does not show the shortest path between two points. The shortest path is located on the great circle (orthodrome). The difference in distance between two lines can reach significant levels depending on the latitude and distance sailed; Especially in high latitudes and long transatlantic routes, this difference can reach hundreds of nautical miles.

Rota ölçümü ile birlikte sıkça kullanıla: One of the concepts frequently used with route measurement is counter route. Countercourse of a route means following the same line in the opposite direction and is found by adding or subtracting 180° to the actual route value.
Rota ölçümü, deniz haritası üzerinde bel: Course measurement is the process of finding the angular value of the direction between two points determined on the sea chart, relative to true north. This process is the concrete equivalent of the concept of direction in navigation on the map and is mandatory for all speed-time-distance calculations to be applied in a correct direction. Route measurement is not just reading an angle; The projection of the map, the meridian structure and the correct reference of the measurement tool used are integral parts of this process.
Rota ölçümü, denizcilikte en temel işlem: Although route measurement seems to be one of the most basic operations in maritime, it is one of the most error-prone issues. Incorrect reference line, angle reading in the wrong direction, or using the wrong scale map can invalidate the entire navigation plan. Therefore, route measurement is not a mechanical ruler movement; It should be considered as a conscious process in which the concept of direction, map structure and mathematical discipline are applied together.
Rota ölçümü, mesafe ölçümü, ölü hesap me: Route measurement, distance measurement, dead reckoning position advancement, bearing intersection and all classical navigation calculations made on the map work with the Mercator projection assumption. Without this projection, no direct relationship could be established between the straight line on the map and the course taken at sea.
Rota ölçümünde harita projeksiyonunun et: The effect of map projection should also be taken into account in route measurement. In the Mercator projection, directions appear as straight lines; This is a huge advantage for fixed route navigation. However, as the distance between meridians increases at high latitudes, measurement accuracy may decrease. In these regions, route measurement should be done more carefully and, if possible, larger scale maps should be preferred.
Rota ölçümünün her zaman uygun ölçekli h: Route measurement should always be done on a map of appropriate scale. The route measured on a small-scale map may be sufficient for general navigation; However, this route should not be used in narrow waters and port approaches without using large-scale maps. The same route line may overlap shoals or obstacles on the large-scale map.
Rota ölçümünün temel mantığı, ölçülecek: The basic logic of route measurement is based on finding the clockwise angle between the route line to be measured and a meridian direction. This angle is expressed between 0° and 360°. The reference line used during measurement must be a meridian; Parallel lines or the map edge can be used as a reference only as long as they are parallel to the meridian direction.

Running Fix yöntemi, aynı sabit objeye f: The Running Fix method is based on finding the location by advancing the bearings taken at different times on the same fixed object using the course and speed of the ship and intersecting the LOPs obtained from these bearings. It is especially used when there is only one suitable object.
Running fix, açık denizde pratik ve işle: Running fix is ​​practical and functional in the open sea; However, if there is a change in route or speed or if DR discipline is poor, the result is not considered reliable. For this reason, the method is not used instead of fixes obtained with simultaneous LOPs whenever possible.
Running fix, akıntı ve rüzgâr etkilerini: Running fix does not take into account current and wind effects. Therefore, the obtained position may deviate from the real position. It should be combined with the EP (Estimated Position) approach in flowing waters.
Running fix, aynı hedefe farklı zamanlar: Running fix is ​​obtained by evaluating two bearings taken at different times to the same target. When the first bearing is taken, the ship's position is on this line, but its exact location is uncertain. When the second bearing is taken after the ship moves, the first bearing is advanced according to the distance and route traveled by the ship. The intersection of this advanced LOP and the second LOP is the running fix.
Running Fix, aynı sabit objeden farklı z: Running Fix is ​​the assignment of position by transferring two or more bearings taken from the same fixed object at different times, taking into account the progress of the ship. It is the basic fix method used in classical (terrestrial) navigation when a single object is present.
Running fix, göksel seyirde **aynı anda: Running fix is ​​based on the principle of moving **position lines (LOP)** that cannot be obtained at the same time** to the same time**, taking into account the movement of the ship in celestial navigation. Observations made at different times are combined into a single time plane to obtain a fix. It is a practical solution when the number of celestial objects is limited or simultaneous observation is not possible due to weather conditions.
Running Fix, tek bir sabit objeden farkl: Running Fix is ​​a method of determining the position by moving two (or more) LOPs taken at different times from a single fixed object as far as the ship's course and the distance traveled. It is one of the basic solutions of classical navigation, especially in coastal areas with a single object and when visibility is limited.
Running fix, tek NAVAID ile iki kerteriz: Running fix determines position using two bearings with a single NAVAID.
Running fix, yalnızca tek bir seyir yard: Running fix is ​​the determination of position using two bearings taken at different times when only a single navigation aid (NAVAID) is visible. According to Bowditch, this method is based on advancing the first bearing line (LOP) as much as the movement of the ship and intersecting it with the second bearing. It is a critical technique when a single lighthouse is visible offshore or when cruising along the coast.

Rüzgâr, gemi üzerinde iki temel hidrodin:
Wind creates two basic hydrodynamic effects on the ship: drag force and lift force. The combination of these two forces affects the course, speed and maneuverability of the ship at sea. Wind effect should be considered as a critical variable both in offshore navigation planning and during maneuvers in ports.

The effect of wind on the ship depends on the ship's freeboard height (side surface area above the water), superstructure shape and loading condition. In the empty ship (ballast) condition, the wind effect is much more pronounced since the freeboard is high; Since the waterline is high and the freeboard is low on a loaded ship, the wind effect is relatively reduced.

Set and drift are two basic parameters used in describing any current (tide, ocean circulation or wind-induced surface drag) from a marine perspective. The set indicates the direction in which the current is moving (in degrees clockwise from true north, the direction in which the current is traveling); Drift refers to the speed of the current (in nautical miles/hour – knots).

This definition is different from wind direction: while the wind is described from the direction it comes from (e.g. a northwest wind comes from the northwest), the current is described from the direction it goes (e.g. a set 090° current flows east). This difference is especially critical when interpreting current and wind effects in the same calculation.

Spring tide (kuvvetli gelgit veya büyük:
Spring tide (strong tide or big tide) is the period when the Moon and the Sun are in the same direction relative to the Earth - during the new moon or full moon period - and the period when the tidal amplitude reaches its highest value. Neap tide (weak tide or small tide) is the period when the Moon and the Sun are perpendicular to each other relative to the Earth - in the first or last quarter period - and the tidal amplitude is at its lowest.

A cycle occurs between these two extremes every 7 days: spring → neap → spring. The periodic nature of the cycle creates a critical planning condition for navigation; A port's tidal window may be much longer during the spring period and much more limited during the neap period.

Squat, ilerleme halindeki bir geminin hı:
Squat is the phenomenon of a ship in progress sinking further into the water than normal due to speed. This phenomenon is explained by the fact that as the ship moves, the bottom water pressure decreases and the flow around the ship pulls the ship down. The actual dynamic draft is calculated by adding the squat value to the ship's draft; This value plays a critical role in UKC calculation.

Squat occurs most clearly in shallow water (shallow water – water depth less than 1.5–2 times the ship's draft) and narrow channels (channel cross-section is limited). In open deep water the squat effect is negligible; However, omitting the squat calculation in channels, dock approaches and shallow sailings can lead to serious UKC errors.

For example, the maximum safe speed for entering a particular channel is calculated so that the squat value remains within the UKC limit. Tidal stream (gelgit akıntısı), denizler:
Tidal stream is the horizontal water movement caused by the periodic water height change (tide) in the seas. Although the tidal movement is up and down, this movement turns into horizontal currents due to the coastal geometry and basin shape. Tidal flowing water is defined by the parameters set (current direction) and drift (current speed, in knots).

Tidal streams are periodic and change direction, unlike permanent currents such as river currents or ocean circulation. In a tidal cycle, the current changes in both speed and direction: it flows in one direction during the falling tide, while the HW begins to flow in the opposite direction with the rising tide after a period of slack water. This periodic character makes the tidal stream predictable; Tidal atlas and current tables provide hourly advance information on currents at each location.

Tidal window (gelgit penceresi), bir gem:
Tidal window is the time period during which sufficient water depth is available for a ship to safely enter or exit a port or canal with a certain draft value. Especially in shallow bars, channel entrances and ports where the tide is decisive, the tidal window forms the center of the entire operational calendar.

Tidal window calculation is a natural continuation of the UKC calculation: the tidal height that satisfies the minimum UKC condition is found and it is determined when this height is exceeded, for how long it is exceeded, and when it falls below it again. This period is the tidal window; The entry/exit operation must be completed within this window.
Tidal window (gelgit penceresi), bir lim: Tidal window is the time period during which the minimum water depth required to enter or exit a port is achieved. The calculation includes the following steps: (1) Minimum required water depth = Draft + Squat + Air allowance + Minimum UKC. (2) Tidal height providing this depth = Minimum required water depth − Chart depth. (3) Using the tidal table and the rule of 12s or the tidal curve, it is calculated when this tidal height is reached and how long it remains above that level.
Tidal window bazı limanlarda ETA’nın en: Tidal window constitutes the strictest restriction of ETA in some ports.
Tidal window belirlendikten sonra liman: Once the tidal window is determined, sufficient time should be left for the port agent, pilot, tugboat and on deck to prepare for the port operation. A realistic tidal window plan includes the following allowances: (1) Early entry allowance: instead of entering immediately after the window opens, waiting an additional 30–60 minutes increases the UKC margin. (2) Operating allowance: unexpected speed losses during transit, traffic delay or pilot coordination time must be taken into account. (3) Margin of safety: tide forecast does not include meteorological influence; Storm surge or low pressure can lower the expected water level by 0.5–1.0 metres. Therefore, meteorology-based water level prediction should also be used during critical transitions.

Trilaterasyon, bir noktanın konumunu, ko:
Trilateration is a method of determining the location of a point using distances to multiple reference points whose location is known. The main difference from triangulation is that triangulation is based on angle measurement, while trilateration is based on distance measurement. GPS applies the principle of trilateration on a global scale; The positions of the satellites are known exactly and the distances to the receiver are measured by signal delay time.

The basic geometric logic of trilateration can be explained as follows: if you are at a distance r₁ from a single point of known location, you can be anywhere on a sphere (or circle in 2D) of radius r₁ centered on that point. When a second reference point is added, the intersection of two spheres creates a circle. Adding the third reference results in two points. Earth conditions make either of these two points meaningless; thus, a single location is determined.
Trilaterasyon, mesafe ölçümünden konum b: Trilateration is a method of determining position from distance measurement; triangulation uses angle.
Trilaterasyonun doğruluğu yalnızca mesaf: The accuracy of trilateration depends not only on distance measurement precision but also on the geometric distribution of reference points (satellites). If the satellites are well distributed in the sky, each measurement provides constraints from different directions and the location is determined precisely. If satellites are clustered together, the reflection of measurement errors to the location becomes larger.

Turn radius is the radius of the circular arc that a ship follows when it makes a full turn at a given rudder angle and speed. Rudder angle, ship speed and hydrodynamic characteristics of the ship determine the turning radius. A small turning radius indicates high maneuverability.

The concept of turning radius is the basic input of route planning in narrow channels, straits and in-harbor maneuvers. How many meters in front of a waypoint a heading change begins depends directly on the turning radius. Ship righting delay (advance) and transverse slip (transfer) amounts are also part of the turning characteristic.

UKC (Under Keel Clearance) is the height of the water column between the ship's keel and the seabed. If this value reaches zero, the ship runs aground; Therefore, UKC is one of the most basic critical indicators of navigational safety. The actual UKC at any given moment is a combination of multiple factors, including chart depth, tide height, ship draft, squat and swell allowance.

UKC calculation is especially critical at port entrances, narrow channels and shallow waters. Most companies set a minimum UKC policy under the ISM Code; This policy is usually expressed as fixed values ​​such as 10–15% of the draft offshore and 0.5–1.0 meters in ports. XTE (Cross Track Error) refers to the vertical (transverse) distance of the ship's current position from the planned route line. If the ship deviates to the right of the course, a positive (+) XTE value is reported, if it deviates to the left, a negative (−) XTE value is reported; Direction sign may vary depending on navigation software. It is automatically calculated and displayed in ECDIS and GPS receivers.

XTE is one of the most basic tracking parameters of passage planning. During the planning phase, the XTE limit is determined for each route segment; This limit refers to the half-width of the safe corridor determined on both sides of the route line. ECDIS generates an alarm when the XTE exceeds this limit.

(2) Local traffic and channel width: in narrow channels or heavy traffic areas, the XTE limit is kept more limited.

Yükleme sırasında ağırlık merkezinin yer: The displacement of the center of gravity during loading depends on the location of the added or removed weights. When a new load is taken on the ship, a new moment is created by multiplying the weight of this load by its vertical distance and is added to the total moment. Likewise, a weight removed from the ship is deducted from the current moment. The new total moment is divided by the new total weight to calculate the current center of gravity. This sequence of operations is always carried out with the same logic and no steps are skipped.

Yüksek basınç merkezi, çevre basınçtan d: A high pressure center is a region where the pressure is higher than the surrounding pressure. Here, air descends from top to bottom and spreads on the surface; The descending air warms up and its moisture capacity increases, thus the cloud dissolves and generally clear, calm weather conditions occur. In the northern hemisphere, the wind rotates clockwise (anticyclonic) around high pressure. High pressure systems are often slow moving or located in semi-permanent positions (Azores High Pressure, Siberian High Pressure, etc.). But high pressure does not always mean calm seas: strong pressure gradients formed at the edges of the system can reach significant wind speeds. Additionally, when high pressure prevails, there is a risk of poor visibility due to radiation fog or inversion layer.
